clips.title: Poland is $499 from catching Italy (IMF, 2031) #Shorts
clips.desc: GDP per person, PPP (IMF WEO Oct 2026): Italy 3× Poland in 1990, 2× in 2008, +9% in 2026, $499 apart in 2031.

clips.title: Italy's economy grew 10% in 25 years. Poland's grew 140% #Shorts
clips.desc: Real GDP, 2000 = 100 (IMF WEO Oct 2026): Italy 110, Germany 130, Spain 150, Poland 240 in 2025.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Four hundred and ninety-nine dollars. {p} That's the gap the IMF now expects between Italy and Poland in 2031: income per person, adjusted for prices. Italy, about seventy-six thousand seven hundred. Poland, about seventy-six thousand two hundred. {pp} In 1990, Italy was more than three times richer than Poland. In 2008, exactly twice as rich. This year, Poland is about nine percent behind: sixty thousand dollars against sixty-six. {p} At this pace, Poland catches a founding member of the European Union, and a G7 country, in about five years.

Poland has done this before. It passed Portugal in 2020. This year, by the IMF's October numbers, it passed Japan. Next year, the forecast says, Spain. Four countries in seven years. {p} Italy is the next name on the list, and it's the biggest one yet: the third-largest economy in the eurozone, home to Ferrari, Fiat and some of the oldest banks in the world. {pp} <soft>So how does a country that was a third as rich as Italy in 1990 end up almost level? It's two stories. One about a country that stopped growing. And one about a country that never stopped.</soft>
Quick one before the two stories: this is a series, and the next episode is Poland versus Germany. When, and whether it happens at all. Subscribe so you don't miss it. {p} Now, Italy.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP, 2000 = 100 (compounded annual growth, NGDP_RPCH)
shots.narration: Here's Italy's economy since 2000, after inflation, with the year 2000 set to one hundred. {p} By 2025, it reaches about a hundred and ten. Ten percent of growth in twenty-five years. Germany managed about thirty. Spain, about fifty. And Poland, on the same chart, about a hundred and forty. {pp} Italy's economy shrank in 2008, 2009, 2012, 2013 and 2020. Between 2008 and 2019, its growth averaged slightly below zero. A lost decade, in the most literal sense. {p} Per person and adjusted for prices, the IMF had Italy at about thirty-nine thousand five hundred dollars in 2008. Seven years later, in 2015: thirty-nine thousand seven hundred. Unchanged. Poland, meanwhile, went from under twenty thousand to twenty-seven.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · general government gross debt (% of GDP), real GDP growth, population (LP)
shots.title: Why Italy stalled
shots.narration: Three numbers tell the story. {p} Debt: Italy's government owes about a hundred and thirty-eight percent of the country's economy this year, among the highest in Europe. A big slice of every budget goes to interest, not investment. {p} Growth: since 2001, Italy has averaged about zero point four percent a year. Poland, about three point six. {p} And people: Italy's population peaked at about sixty point three million in 2014. This year it's about fifty-eight point nine, and the IMF expects it to keep falling. Fewer workers, more retirees.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Now Poland. {p} Since 1992, Poland's economy has grown every single year except one: 2020, the pandemic. Thirty-three years, one recession, and that one lasted a single year. {p} The average since 2001 is about three and a half percent a year. Never spectacular. Just relentless. {pp} On this chart, it passes Portugal in 2020 and, in the IMF's forecast, Spain next year. {p} Why? Poland joined the European Union in 2004 and has been the biggest net recipient of EU money ever since: roads, rail, factories. It kept its own currency, the złoty, which fell in every crisis and kept Polish exports cheap. And it became the workshop of German industry: car parts, appliances, batteries, built in Poland and sold across Europe.

There's a second reason, and it's less flattering for Italy. {p} Half of this chart is Poland running. The other half is Italy standing still. Catching up is always two numbers: how fast you run, and how fast the other guy runs. {p} Between 2008 and 2019, Poland's economy grew about forty-nine percent. Italy's shrank. That is the whole gap, right there.
Now, the catch. Because Italy isn't poor, and a chart like this hides a few things. {p} And if you're enjoying this, the subscribe button is right there. The series continues.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ (NGDPDPC), 2026 and 2031
shots.title: Per person, plain US$
shots.narration: Everything so far was adjusted for prices. In plain dollars, Italy is still well ahead: about forty-six thousand per person this year, against thirty-one thousand for Poland. Italy is about forty-seven percent richer on that measure. {p} And the IMF still has Italy ahead in 2031: about fifty-two thousand against forty-two. The plain-dollar gap closes too, just more slowly: from about forty-seven percent this year to about twenty-four percent in 2031. {pp} Prices in Poland are lower, so a Polish salary buys more at home. That's what the price-adjusted numbers capture, and it's the fairer comparison of living standards. But if you're buying a German car or a flight to New York, you pay in plain dollars. And there, Italy still wins. {p} Italy also has something no growth chart shows: decades of accumulated wealth. Housing, savings, infrastructure, brands the whole world knows. Poland is catching up on income. Wealth takes a generation longer.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth 2027–2031, population (LP), government gross debt (% of GDP)
shots.title: The IMF's 2027–2031 forecast
shots.narration: So does Poland actually pass Italy? {p} The IMF's forecast runs to 2031, and in 2031 Poland is still four hundred and ninety-nine dollars short: ninety-nine point three percent of Italy's level. The crossing, if it comes, sits just past the edge of the forecast, around 2032. {pp} And the forecast already has Poland slowing down: about two and a half percent a year from 2027, against about zero point six for Italy. {p} Poland has headwinds of its own. Its population is shrinking too, from about thirty-eight million in 2000 to about thirty-six this year. And its government debt is climbing fast, from about sixty-seven percent of the economy this year to about eighty-two by 2031, partly because Poland now spends more on defense, as a share of its economy, than any other NATO member.

Still, the direction hasn't changed in thirty-five years. {p} Since 1991, Poland has gained on Italy in thirty-two years out of thirty-six, through two global recessions and a pandemic. And since 2002, it lost ground only twice, in 2021 and 2023, each time by a fraction of a point. {p} That's thirty-five years of one direction. So even if the crossing slips to 2033 or 2034, this chart only goes one way.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: And after Italy, the list keeps going. {p} In 2031, the IMF has Poland at about ninety-five percent of Britain's level, and ninety-five percent of France's. Germany is further out, at about eighty-three percent. Britain and France, two of the big four of Western Europe, within five percent. Thirty-five years ago, Poland was about a third of all three. {pp} If the 2010s and 2020s repeat, the 2030s are the decade Poland catches the big three of Western Europe. If Italy finally grows again, the race gets interesting. {p} Either way, the map of Europe's richest countries is being redrawn, and it's being redrawn from the east.

<soft>Which one do you think Poland passes first after Italy: Britain or France?</soft> Tell me in the comments. {p} If you're watching from Italy: what would it take to get Italy growing again? {p} And if you're watching from Poland: which country should I cover next? I read every comment.
Spain is the one Poland passes next year, and this year the gap is fifty-five dollars. That whole story is right here. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Poland Just Passed Japan. Italy Is Next.
yt.description:
In 1990 Italy was more than three times richer than Poland per person, adjusted for prices. In 2008, exactly twice. In the IMF's October 2026 World Economic Outlook, Poland is 9% behind this year and $499 behind in 2031, after passing Portugal (2020), Japan (2026) and, in the forecast, Spain (2027). Italy's 25 years of near-zero growth, Poland's 33 years with one recession, the plain-dollar catch, whether the crossing actually happens, and who comes after Italy.
